Executive Overview

Customer-level analysis uses a dataset modeled for analytical demonstration (50,000 user records). Spotify public reports are used for business context. Nothing here is Spotify proprietary data or Spotify's actual strategy.

Customer segmentation

Who are Spotify's customers?

Four segments from K-Prototypes clustering on 11 mixed inputs. Ad interaction and ad conversion were left out of the inputs and analysed afterwards.

Descriptive

Segment profile index

100 = average across all 50,000 users
Index = segment average ÷ full-dataset average × 100. Recent activity = share not inactive 3+ months. Premium share = share on any paid plan. Sessions: Not available from current dataset.

Targeting strategy

From segments to marketing actions

Ad response is statistically the same across segments, so targeting follows each segment's marketing objective rather than a predicted ad lift.

Recommendation
Read this asMarketing recommendations derived from patterns in an analytical dataset. They are not claims about Spotify's actual internal strategy. Each action should be validated with a controlled test (for example, an A/B holdout per segment) before rollout.
Methodology

How the analysis was done

Data, segmentation, outcome definitions and statistical tests, with the line between description, inference and recommendation kept explicit.

Analytical framework

50,000 usersCustomer-level dataset
Customer profilingAge, country, plan, device
Behavioural analyticsListening, playlists, skips, inactivity, rating
SegmentationK-Prototypes, k = 4
Ad interactionOutcome 1, after segmentation
Ad conversionOutcome 2, among interactors
TargetingObjective per segment

Data

  • 50,000 customer records, 17 usable variables (one empty column dropped).
  • Countries: 12. Genres: 12. Plans: Free, Student, Premium Individual, Duo, Family.
  • Ages 16–60. Under-18 kept as its own group. 65+: Not available from current dataset.
  • No dates, sessions, revenue or ad impressions, so no time trends. KPI indicators compare the filtered view with all users instead.

Segmentation

  • Preferred method: TwoStep Cluster (SPSS). It is not available outside SPSS, so K-Prototypes (Huang, 1998) was used. It handles mixed numeric and categorical data the same way.
  • Numeric inputs (z-scored): age, listening hours, playlists, skips, months inactive, recommendation rating.
  • Categorical inputs: country, genre, subscription type, device, most-liked feature.
  • Excluded: ad interaction, ad conversion (outcomes).
  • Fitted on a 15,000-user random sample, then all 50,000 users were assigned.

Choosing k

The cost curve falls smoothly with no sharp elbow, so natural cluster structure is weak. k = 4 was chosen because its profiles are distinct and easy to interpret. Segment names come from rules on each profile, not from assumptions.

Outcomes

  • Ad interaction rate = interacted ÷ all users.
  • Ad-to-subscription rate = converted ÷ ad-interacting users (headline conversion metric).
  • Overall conversion rate = converted ÷ all users.
  • Data flag: 1,921 converted users still show plan = Free (likely snapshot timing).

Statistical tests

  • Chi-square tests of independence: 8 categorical variables × 2 outcomes. Cramér's V reported as the effect size.
  • Binary logistic regression on ad conversion among 17,486 interactors, with odds ratios, 95% CIs and p-values.
  • No result is presented as significant unless p < 0.05. Results that do not survive a Bonferroni correction are flagged as exploratory.

Three kinds of claim

  • Descriptive What the data shows (counts, rates, averages). It updates with the filters.
  • Inferential Whether a difference is larger than chance. Full dataset, static.
  • Recommendation Marketing judgement drawn from the above. Not Spotify policy.
